attrs.label: Ciphera ID
attrs.heading: The sign-in <br class="hidden sm:inline">behind Ciphera.
attrs.body: Ciphera ID is infrastructure, not a product. It is how you sign in to Ciphera's own applications — with a password that never reaches our servers and a profile we cannot read.

attrs.label: 01 · What it is
attrs.heading: One account for our applications.

text.text: Every Ciphera application shares one account. You sign in once at id.ciphera.net and arrive back at the application you came from over OAuth 2.0 with mandatory PKCE. Today that means Pulse, with more of our own services to follow. Ciphera ID does the authentication ceremonies — sign in, sign up, recovery — and nothing else; your settings live in the application you are using.
It is not a general-purpose identity platform, and we would rather say so on this page than let you find out after a procurement call:

attrs.trailingText: If you want to build on this model, the part you can actually use is Tessera — the OPAQUE implementation underneath Ciphera ID, published open-source under Apache-2.0.

bullets.text: No self-serve client registration — adding an application takes a database migration by us
No OpenID Connect discovery document and no JWKS endpoint for third-party token verification
No “Sign in with Ciphera” SDK, no social-login connectors, no SAML
No plan, no price and no checkout — the billing tables were removed rather than left dormant

attrs.label: 02 · Authentication
attrs.heading: Your password never leaves your device.

text.text: With OPAQUE (RFC 9807), your password is stretched on your device with Argon2id and proven to our servers without ever being sent. We store only an opaque credential record that can't be reversed into your password — so even a full database breach gives attackers nothing usable.

bullets.text: OPAQUE (RFC 9807) — your password is never sent to our servers
We store only an opaque credential record — no password, hash, or verifier
No password reset — recovery runs on a 24-word phrase we never see

attrs.note: To be precise about the last one: there is no email reset, because there is nothing on our side to reset. Recovery runs on the 24-word phrase shown at the end of signup — it enrols a second identity that we cannot read, and it is the only thing besides your password that can open the account. Accounts created before 7 September 2026 set it up from Security settings, which needs the password, so do it while you still have it. Lose the password with no phrase enrolled and the account is gone — for us as much as for anyone.

rows.note: Keyed hash — not reversible to an address
Credential record — no password inside it
Inert without a key only your device derives
Ciphertext — your name and email, sealed

attrs.tableTitle: What an operator with full database access sees
attrs.tableSubtitle: One account row, in its entirety
attrs.note: The trade-off is real and we take it deliberately: because we cannot read your address, we cannot reset your password for you, and a lawful order served on us returns ciphertext. The full account of what we can and cannot see is in what we see about you.
attrs.label: 03 · The vault
attrs.heading: We do not know your name or your email address.
attrs.text: This is the part that surprises people, so it is worth being literal about it. The account table has no email column and no name column. Your name and email are sealed in a vault encrypted on your own device, under a key derived during the OPAQUE exchange that our servers never hold in usable form. To find your account at sign-in we use a blind index — a keyed hash of your email that identifies the row without revealing the address.

attrs.label: 04 · Sessions
attrs.heading: What happens after you sign in.
attrs.dek: Applications never see your credentials. They receive a short-lived token over an OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow, and they verify it without calling back to us on every request.

items.title: OAuth 2.0, PKCE mandatory
items.body: Every authorization-code flow requires PKCE with S256 — there is no downgrade path and no implicit flow. Access tokens live 15 minutes; refresh tokens rotate on use, and a reused token revokes the family.

items.title: A log you can read, on data we hash
items.body: Every sign-in, password change and second-factor event is recorded, and you can end any session from your account settings. Client IP addresses are HMAC-hashed before they are written — which is why the log shows a mask, not an address.

bullets.text: TOTP two-factor authentication with any authenticator app
Escalating lockout on repeated failures (15 min → 1 hour → 24 hours)
A captcha challenge after three failed attempts
Expired tokens and stale sessions cleaned up automatically

attrs.label: 05 · Data residency
attrs.heading: Hosted in Switzerland. Blind by design.

text.text: All identity data is stored under the Federal Act on Data Protection (FADP). Passwords use zero-knowledge OPAQUE auth, IPs are HMAC-hashed, and audit logs are batched asynchronously — privacy at every layer.

bullets.text: Run on our own infrastructure — no third-party identity vendor holds your account
Automatic token cleanup and session expiration
Security alerts rate-limited to 1 per hour per user

attrs.imageAlt: Zurich, Switzerland — where Ciphera data is hosted

attrs.label: 06 · The code
attrs.heading: You cannot buy this. You can read it.
attrs.body: Ciphera ID is an internal service, and it is staying that way. The cryptography underneath it is not: Tessera is the same OPAQUE code that verifies real Ciphera sign-ins, published under Apache-2.0 for anyone who wants to hold no passwords either.
